time.desc: National security authorities filed documents in a federal appeals court publicly detailing accusations that short-video platforms pose a national security threat and requesting that the platforms’ legal challenges be dismissed.

The management department of the national legislative body announced that it will remove all applications owned by the parent company from its managed devices within a time limit, expanding the scope of the original ban.

Federal law enforcement and consumer privacy watchdogs filed a civil lawsuit against the short video platform and its parent company, accusing it of illegally collecting data from children under the age of majority and violating children's privacy regulations.

Institution B and supervision Institution B filed a lawsuit against Platform X and Parent Company Y in Court G, accusing them of allowing children under 13 years of age to create accounts since 2019, illegally collecting children's personal information and interacting with adult users without parental consent, and continuing to collect and retain it after the court had previously ordered a ban; Platform X denied the accusations, saying that many of the accusations involved past practices that had been corrected.

The short video platform submitted documents to the federal court to formally challenge the "stripping or banning" law, claiming that the law infringes on freedom of speech and disclosed its local data and content governance arrangements.
Many senior government officials and governors joined the short video platform in advance of the political party conference and quickly gained millions of views.
A federal appeals court held its first oral argument on the "strive or ban" law, as platforms and governments battle over free speech and national security risks.
The platform announced the closure of its music streaming service, shrinking its business front and concentrating resources to cope with the survival crisis.

Several states and regions jointly sued the short video platform, accusing its addictive products of being designed to harm minors and misleading the public about the effectiveness of content moderation and safety measures.

Internal platform documents blackened in the lawsuit were restored and leaked, showing that executives knew the algorithm was harmful to children and planned to use the content to gain support from lawmakers

Platform X Spokesperson Seventeen issued a statement for the first time regarding the accidental leakage of 30 pages of confidential internal documents due to a blackout defect in a state lawsuit. The documents showed that its executives knew that the algorithm was harmful to children and that ordinary users would become 'addicted' after about 35 minutes of use. The spokesman defended the company's child safety record, condemned the release of now-sealed material as "extremely irresponsible", and accused the lawsuit of taking out of context, citing misleading statements and using outdated documents.
